title: Update on chemotherapy modalities for retinoblastoma: Progress and challenges
clinical_background: Retinoblastoma is the most common childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without prompt treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, detection usually precedes invasion of surrounding structures and disease-free survival approaches 100%; in low-and-middle-income countries, presentation with invasive disease is more common and survival is substantially lower. Treatment has evolved from a primary emphasis on survival toward preserving eyes and vision while limiting complications. Chemotherapy delivered through several routes is central to this approach, but the choice of treatment depends on the clinical circumstances.
objectives: Summarize current knowledge and emerging trends in chemotherapy for retinoblastoma across different administration routes.
Review treatment considerations, doses, administration methods, outcomes, and potential complications.
Examine emerging treatments and future directions intended to improve treatment outcomes.
study_design: Narrative review informed by a PubMed search for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, with a focus on publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma and intravenous, intra-arterial, intravitreal, intracameral, and periocular chemotherapy, as well as chemoreduction and ophthalmic artery chemosurgery.

population.description: Children with retinoblastoma, including intraocular and extraocular disease.

interpretation: The review presents chemotherapy as the central globe-preserving treatment for retinoblastoma, within care that may also require surgery, radiotherapy or focal treatment. The authors consider systemic IVC particularly important for bilateral or germline disease, whereas targeted IAC is often favored for unilateral or non-germline disease and may salvage eyes after other treatments fail. IvitC, ICC and periocular chemotherapy can address selected sites of persistent disease as adjuncts. The preferred route depends on disease and patient characteristics, treatment availability, cost and family preference; no single approach is optimal for every patient.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The review attributes established globe-salvage outcomes with IVC to earlier cohorts, while noting that a meta-analysis found two-drug intravenous regimens less effective across retinoblastoma stages and enhanced regimens more effective than standard IVC in eyes with vitreous seeds. Another meta-analysis favored IAC over IVC for globe salvage in group D eyes (79.5% versus 55%; P < 0.001), but found no significant difference in group E eyes (51% versus 43%, respectively). Reported recurrence and metastasis rates after IAC (15% and 2.7%, respectively) were not significantly different from those after IVC (15% and 0.6%, respectively). Prior studies also support intravitreal treatment for vitreous seeds, intracameral treatment for aqueous seeds and periocular topotecan as an option associated with fewer complications than periocular carboplatin.
clinical_implications: For bilateral or germline retinoblastoma, IVC provides intraocular treatment alongside the systemic protection that the authors attribute to it, including prevention of metastasis and reduction of long-term second malignancies.

For unilateral or non-germline disease, IAC concentrates treatment in the affected eye and may reduce systemic toxicity relative to IVC; unlike IVC, however, it does not provide systemic chemoprotective effects.
Vitreous and aqueous seeding can remain barriers to globe preservation despite other treatment routes; IvitC and ICC offer local adjunctive options in selected cases.
IAC outcomes and complications may vary with access to specialized facilities and endovascular expertise.
practice_implications: Tailor the chemotherapy route to age, stage, laterality, germline status, treatment availability, financial considerations and family preference.

Use IVC primarily for bilateral or germline retinoblastoma, as described by the authors; IAC is often preferred initially for unilateral or non-germline disease and can be used after chemoreduction or another intervention fails.

Examine the enucleated eye histopathologically to guide risk stratification and decisions about adjuvant treatment; the cited Children's Oncology Group findings suggest that eyes with less than 3 mm choroidal involvement and any prelaminar/laminar optic nerve invasion may not need adjuvant chemotherapy, whereas extensive choroidal and significant post-laminar optic nerve invasion warrant a more intensive adjuvant IVC regimen.

Reserve IvitC chiefly for refractory or recurrent vitreous seeds after other therapy, with careful examination and safety-enhanced injection techniques; tumor at the injection site, pars plana invasion and anterior chamber seeding are contraindications described in the review.
Consider ICC for aqueous seeding only in carefully selected patients treated by trained, experienced ocular oncologists.
Weigh IAC's potential visual benefit against its vascular and systemic risks, particularly in advanced disease, and use clinicians with specialized endovascular experience.
limitations: The authors describe the published evidence on extraocular retinoblastoma treatment as limited.
IAC lacks standardized protocols and universally agreed drug combinations and doses, and its technical demands may contribute to variation between centers.
Evidence for pIvitC comes from a limited number of treated eyes, and the technique is difficult to perform and has not been widely adopted.

The review describes tandem IAC as controversial because of possible vascular toxicity in the better-seeing eye, uncertainty about pineoblastoma prevention and limited efficacy against existing metastases.
open_questions: Which IAC regimen and dosing schedule should be standardized remains unresolved.
The benefits and risks of tandem IAC in advanced bilateral disease remain uncertain.
The mechanisms of chemotherapy resistance are complex and may differ from resistance to individual drugs.
The long-term implications of novel targeted treatment approaches require further investigation.
future_directions: Phase I trials of the sustained-release topotecan episcleral plaque Chemoplaque for residual or recurrent active disease after first-line treatment (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT04156347 and NCT04428879) are assessing safety primarily and efficacy secondarily.

Investigational approaches discussed by the authors include molecularly targeted treatment, immunotherapy, gene therapy, angiogenesis inhibition, aqueous humor markers, exosomes and MLN4924 (pevonedistat).
Retinoblastoma organoid findings identify sunitinib as a potential candidate for further study in RB1-deficient and MYCN-amplified disease.
Drug-delivery research includes NPs, fibrin glue, a dual-layer hydrogel implant and other intraocular carriers intended to improve targeted or sustained chemotherapy delivery.
Further investigation of the long-term effects of novel therapies is needed, particularly as treatments for advanced disease develop.

notable_adverse_events: For IVC, the review characterizes systemic toxicity as minimal and long-term hearing and renal complications as uncommon when treatment is administered precisely.

A cited IVC report documented hearing loss, including pre-existing cases (4%); growth abnormalities, primarily associated with 13Q syndrome (6%); transient vincristine-related neuropathy (2%); and hematological effects including neutropenia, anemia and thrombocytopenia. It found no significant differences in systemic adverse events across ICRB A–E severity groups.

Table 1 reports febrile neutropenia (29) for Chung et al.; febrile neutropenia (38), myelosuppression (40), constitutional symptoms (17) and one secondary osteosarcoma (4) for Bartuma et al.; and transient anemia (11), pancytopenia (6) and thrombocytopenia (4) for Manjandavida et al. These figures appear under the table's complications (%) heading.

Table 1 reports neutropenia (22), thrombocytopenia (26), anemia (13) and allergy to carboplatin (9) for Munier et al.; rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (10) for Yousef et al.; and myelosuppression (70) for Wen et al. These figures appear under the table's complications (%) heading.

Table 1 also reports hearing loss (4), growth abnormality (6), transient vincristine neuropathy (2), pineoblastoma (2), metastasis (2) and death (1) among the reported outcomes for the Shields et al. 2020 cohort; the prose identifies pre-existing hearing-loss cases and primarily associates growth abnormalities with 13Q syndrome. The document does not attribute the reported death to treatment.
For IAC, commonly self-resolving ocular effects are periocular edema and hyperemia (34%), ptosis (13.5%), focal madarosis (10.5%) and forehead erythema (3%).

In an experienced IAC team reported by Shields et al., retinal ischemia (1%), choroidal ischemia (1%) and neovascularization of the disc, retina or iris, or glaucoma (approximately 1% each) were documented.

Neutropenia has been reported with IAC but is described as less frequent than with IVC. Reported procedural risks include femoral artery occlusion, blue toe syndrome, hematoma, arterial occlusion, stroke and transient ischemic attack; the review states that femoral artery occlusion and blue toe syndrome can be reversed with anticoagulation.

For intravitreal chemotherapy, retinal pigment mottling at the injection site is reported in 18–43% of cases. Higher doses, particularly 50 μg of melphalan, have been associated with rare severe hypotony and phthisis bulbi, sometimes requiring enucleation. Less frequent reported effects include iris atrophy, chorioretinal atrophy, transient vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment.
The suggested greater melphalan-related toxicity in more deeply pigmented eyes is presented as a concern and speculation, not as an established comparative finding.

Table 4 reports localized peripheral salt-and-pepper retinopathy (43) with Munier et al.'s intravitreal Melphalan series; VH (2) with the Muier et al. Melphalan and Carboplatin series; and hypotonia (22), temporary epithelial defect (11) and VH (11) with the Ghassemi et al. Melphalan and Topotecan series. These figures appear under complications (%).

Table 4 reports VH (6) and intraretinal heme (6) for Francis et al.; focal retinal pigment epithelial mottling (18) and non-axial posterior lens opacity (18) for the Shields et al. 11-eye series; and focal retinal pigment epithelial mottling (54), minor focal paraxial lens opacity (28), VH (12.5), retinal hemorrhage (5), optic disc edema (3), hemorrhagic retinal necrosis (3) and transient hypotony (8) for the Shields et al. 40-eye series. These figures appear under complications (%).

Table 4 reports VH (10), retinal pigment epithelium and choroid atrophy (63), iris atrophy (40), posterior synechiae (43), retinal vascular occlusion (40), optic atrophy (20), persistent hypotonia and phthisis bulbi (13), and cataracts (27) for the Xue et al. intravitreal Melphalan series. These figures appear under complications (%).

Table 4 reports cataract (6), pigmentary retinopathy (53), anterior uveitis (33) and pupillary synechiae (53) for Amin et al.; macular or pan-retinopathy with optic atrophy (14) for Berry et al.; and VH (10), pigmentary retinopathy (4), chorioretinal atrophy (3) and posterior synechiae (3) for Kiratli et al. These figures appear under complications (%).

Table 4 reports retinal hemorrhage (4), pupillary synechiae (15), cataracts (30), iris atrophy (7), and retinopathy and optic atrophy (4) for Yousef et al.; hypotony (9), cataract (9) and severe pigment dispersion (5) for Riazi-Esfahani; and VH (18), retinal hemorrhage (18), pupillary synechiae (7), cataracts (15) and iris atrophy (4) for Alahmadi et al. These figures appear under complications (%).

For intracameral chemotherapy, cited studies reported minimal anterior-segment toxicity and no evidence of extraocular tumor spread. Reported adverse effects include iris heterochromia and progressive cataracts.

Periocular carboplatin is associated in cited reports with substantial local adverse effects, including orbital fibrosis and optic nerve atrophy. Reported eyelid edema and conjunctival chemosis after periocular topotecan were transient.

subgroup_analyses: IVC outcomes differed by eye classification in the Shields et al. cohorts: preservation was highest in groups A–C, lower in group D, and limited or absent in group E, depending on the cohort and selection of group E eyes.
In the cited meta-analysis, group D globe salvage favored IAC over IVC (79.5% versus 55%; P < 0.001), whereas the group E comparison (51% versus 43%) was not significant.
For group E eyes, IAC with intravitreal chemotherapy reduced enucleation relative to IAC alone (27% versus 73%; P = 0.04).
In Liang et al.'s primary-IAC study of advanced unilateral disease, 3-year ocular survival was significantly higher for group D than for group E (97% versus 76%; P < 0.01).
The cited IVC safety report found no significant difference in systemic adverse events across ICRB A–E groups.
The IAC outcomes assessed by Shields et al. varied minimally by age, race and sex; the article provides no subgroup estimates for those characteristics.
secondary_results: A cited report found no published evidence that IVC adversely affects fertility; this is an absence of evidence, not a demonstration of no effect.
The review states that IVC helps prevent metastasis and reduce long-term second cancers and pineoblastoma, without providing an effect estimate for these outcomes.
The review reports that IAC entails shorter chemotherapy exposure and less systemic toxicity than IVC, but does not provide an overall comparative toxicity rate.

Because IAC delivers treatment locally, the review states that it does not provide systemic chemoprotective effects in other organs; systemic micrometastasis remains a concern in advanced intraocular or extraocular disease.

The cited intracameral studies found that clear corneal or limbal delivery of melphalan (15–20 μg/0.05 ml) and topotecan (7.5 μg/0.015 ml) could control aqueous seeding, with minimal anterior-segment toxicity and no reported extraocular spread.
Periocular chemotherapy is reported to achieve vitreous levels within 30 min and doses 6–10 times greater than those attainable intravenously, with an effect lasting for hours.

A cited retinoblastoma-organoid study identified sunitinib as cytotoxic against RB1-deficient and MYCN-amplified organoids and reported inhibited proliferation and induced differentiation; these are organoid findings, not clinical outcomes.
Phase I evaluations of the sustained-release topotecan episcleral plaque Chemoplaque (NCT04156347 and NCT04428879) are described as ongoing; the review provides no trial results.

main_conclusion: The authors regard chemotherapy as the principal first-line approach to preserving the eye in retinoblastoma, within multimodal care. They favor tailoring the administration route to age, stage, laterality, germline status, access, cost, and family preference: IVC is central for bilateral or germline disease, IAC is often preferred initially for unilateral or non-germline disease and can be used after other treatment fails, while IvitC, ICC, and periocular delivery are adjuncts for selected cases.
narrative_summary: This review searched PubMed literature on retinoblastoma chemotherapy and examined intravenous, intraarterial, intravitreal, intracameral, and periocular delivery, including administration, outcomes, and complications. Its authors describe chemotherapy as the foundation of eye-preserving treatment, while emphasizing that route selection depends on disease and patient characteristics, treatment availability, cost, and family preference. In a cited meta-analysis, Group D globe preservation favored IAC over IVC, at 79.5% versus 55% (P < 0.001); the corresponding Group E comparison, 51% versus 43%, was not significant. IVC remains important for bilateral or germline disease and for systemic protection, whereas IAC delivers treatment locally but does not provide the same potential protection elsewhere in the body. For refractory or recurrent vitreous seeds, intravitreal therapy can support globe salvage when patient selection and injection safeguards are meticulous. Intracameral chemotherapy addresses selected cases with aqueous seeds, and periocular chemotherapy provides another adjunctive route. The authors note ocular and systemic toxicities, procedural risks, and the specialized expertise required for local delivery. They conclude that multimodal, individually selected treatment is necessary to preserve life, eyes, and vision. Emerging molecular therapies, gene therapy, and drug-delivery systems may improve outcomes, but their longer-term implications require further study.

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Retinoblastoma treatment has shifted from prioritizing survival alone toward preserving eyes and vision while limiting treatment complications. Chemotherapy remains central to care. In addition to intravenous chemotherapy (IVC), intraarterial (IAC), intravitreal, intracameral, and periocular delivery offer treatment options. Studies have reported globe salvage approaching 100% for groups A–C. For advanced intraocular disease in groups D and E, IAC appears to provide better local control than IVC. Carefully performed intravitreal chemotherapy may help patients with vitreous seeds avoid enucleation and radiotherapy. Route selection depends on multiple patient and disease factors. This review examines administration, doses, outcomes, complications, emerging treatments, and future directions.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Retinoblastoma is the most frequent childhood ocular malignancy and affects approximately 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births. Without timely treatment, it can be fatal. In high-income countries, diagnosis generally precedes invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or orbit, and disease-free survival approaches 100%. In low-and-middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, invasive presentation is more common, increasing local and distant metastatic risk and substantially lowering survival. Treatment aims to preserve life, prevent metastasis, retain the eye, and maximize vision, although protocols differ between centers. Before the 1990 s, enucleation and external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) predominated but could cause vision loss and serious adverse effects. Subsequent approaches improved disease-free survival, globe salvage, and, in selected cases, vision preservation. Plaque radiotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and transpupillary thermotherapy contributed to this change, while chemotherapy delivered by different routes had a particularly important role. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles dating back to January 1, 1960, targeting publications from January 1, 1990, to January 31, 2024. Search terms covered retinoblastoma, chemotherapy, intravenous chemotherapy, chemoreduction, intra-arterial chemotherapy, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery, intravitreal chemotherapy, intracameral chemotherapy, and periocular chemotherapy. Their aim was to summarize current knowledge and emerging chemotherapy trends in retinoblastoma.

document_sections.heading: 2. Intravenous chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Kingston et al. observed in the early 1990 s that a chemotherapy protocol repurposed from neuroblastoma could treat retinoblastoma; later studies supported that observation. Systemic IVC remains important and is called chemoreduction because it consistently decreases tumor size. Treatment generally gives 2, 3, or 4 agents monthly for 6–9 consecutive cycles. A commonly used protocol combines vincristine, etoposide, and carboplatin (VEC), frequently with thermotherapy or cryotherapy for focal consolidation. IVC controls intraocular disease and can prevent metastasis and reduce subsequent second cancers and pineoblastoma. Protocol selection varies by center. IVC is generally used for bilateral, familial, or germline mutation retinoblastoma; for children aged 4 months or younger when IAC is difficult; and when early optic nerve or choroidal invasion is suspected. It may also be considered when IAC is unavailable or according to family preferences. Histopathological examination after enucleation is important for risk assessment. Extraocular extension, extensive peripapillary choroidal involvement (≥3 mm), and post-laminar optic nerve invasion (≥1.5 mm) substantially increase metastatic risk. Children's Oncology Group (COG) studies suggest that eyes with less than 3 mm choroidal involvement and any prelaminar/laminar optic nerve invasion have little recurrence risk and may not need adjuvant chemotherapy. Extensive choroidal and substantial post-laminar optic nerve invasion are associated with worse outcomes and call for more intensive adjuvant IVC. In 2006, Shields et al. studied 249 cases receiving intravenous VEC and reported tumor control with globe salvage in 100% of group A eyes, 93% of group B, 90% of group C, and 47% of group D; group E required enucleation. In 2020, Shields et al. assessed 964 eyes from 554 patients treated with similar chemotherapy. Following a 6-cycle VEC regimen, Kaplan-Meier analysis found control without enucleation or EBRT within 3 years in groups A (96%), B (91%), C (91%), D (71%), and selected E eyes (32%); results were generally maintained over 20 years. Standard IVC uses six VEC cycles with stage-adjusted doses. Reduced regimens use two agents, such as VE, VC, or EC, to limit adverse effects; enhanced regimens add potentially more toxic second-line agents or extend treatment beyond six cycles to improve globe salvage. A meta-analysis by Daniels et al. found two-drug regimens less effective across retinoblastoma stages. It found enhanced regimens more effective than standard IVC for eyes with vitreous seeds, indicating a possible role when IAC is unavailable. Table 1 summarizes reported intraocular IVC outcomes and complications. Adding IAC and plaque radiotherapy has increased globe salvage by 5–28%. Intravitreal and intracameral chemotherapy can improve local seed control and overall globe salvage. Adding intravitreal melphalan to IVC may also reduce the need for repeated examinations under anesthesia. IVC generally has limited systemic toxicity; lasting auditory and renal complications are uncommon, especially with precise administration. One report documented hearing loss, including pre-existing cases (4%); growth abnormalities, mainly associated with 13Q syndrome (6%); transient neuropathy related to vincristine (2%); and anticipated neutropenia, anemia, or thrombocytopenia. That study found no significant difference in systemic adverse events among ICRB A–E severity groups. Published literature provides no evidence that IVC adversely affects fertility. Extraocular disease is uncommon in developed countries but more frequent in developing countries and has poorer visual and survival outcomes than intraocular disease. Current treatment generally combines high-dose neoadjuvant chemotherapy, enucleation or exenteration, EBRT, and adjuvant chemotherapy. Evidence for extraocular retinoblastoma remains limited, and approaches are evolving; Table 2 summarizes reported systemic IVC outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 3. Intraarterial chemotherapy
document_sections.content: IAC, also called super-selective ophthalmic artery chemotherapy or chemosurgery, is widely used as primary retinoblastoma treatment. In 1998, Kaneko et al. described delivery of melphalan through the ophthalmic artery using a micro-balloon catheter advanced transfemorally to the cervical internal carotid artery beyond the ophthalmic artery origin; they called it selective ophthalmic artery infusion. In 2006, Gobin et al. introduced guide-wire catheterization directly into the ophthalmic artery, termed super-selective intra-ophthalmic artery chemotherapy, to improve drug delivery. Abramson et al. reported in 2008 that most patients in their initial experience retained the eye with little systemic or local toxicity. Early IAC mainly used melphalan alone because of its activity against retinoblastoma and evidence from rabbits of good vitreous and retinal penetration. Francis et al. investigated a two-drug regimen; Abramson et al. and Marr et al. later introduced melphalan with carboplatin and topotecan, a combination adopted for its potential efficacy and favorable safety. No standardized IAC protocol, drug combination, or dose has universal agreement. Care commonly consists of three sessions four weeks apart, although reports include up to 11 sessions; the median across studies is three. Two- or three-agent combinations are common. To deliver melphalan safely and effectively, doses should remain below 0.5 mg/ kg, typically 3–7.5 mg. Children's Oncology Group (COG) age-based doses are 3 mg for 6–12 months, 3.5 mg for 12–24 months, and 4 mg for children over 24 months, accounting for increasing eye volume. Other commonly used combination doses are topotecan 0.5–2 mg and carboplatin 15–30 mg. Further IAC sessions can be considered for selected responses, but transpupillary thermotherapy or cryotherapy after IAC is often preferred to obtain complete regression while balancing control against local and visual toxicity. Primary IAC is generally indicated for unilateral groups B, C, and D (cT1b, cT2, cT3, cT4) and bilateral groups D and E (cT3). Secondary use can address recurrent or persistent tumor, subretinal seeds, or their combination after treatment failure. Tandem, simultaneous bilateral IAC has also been used in advanced bilateral cases with less than two cycles of exposure, but remains controversial. Concerns include vascular injury to the better-seeing eye, uncertain pineoblastoma prevention, and limited activity against existing metastases, potentially increasing child mortality. For groups B and C, reported globe salvage with IAC ranges from 95% to 100%, comparable to IVC. A meta-analysis found higher group D globe salvage with IAC than IVC (79.5% versus 55%; P < 0.001), but no significant group E difference (51% versus 43%, respectively). Combining IAC with intravitreal chemotherapy reduced enucleation compared with IAC alone (15% versus 44%, P = 0.01), particularly in group E (27% versus 73%, P = 0.04). After an average of three IAC sessions, Shields et al. reported complete control of solid tumors in 88%, subretinal seeds in 82%, and vitreous seeds in 67%. A comparison found that recurrence and metastasis after IAC (15% and 2.7%, respectively) did not differ significantly from rates after IVC (15% and 0.6%, respectively). Liang et al. reported greater 3-year ocular survival after primary IAC for advanced unilateral group D than group E disease (97% versus 76%; P < 0.01). Vitreous hemorrhage was common in that study; no deaths or severe systemic complications were reported. Table 3 presents IAC regimens, outcomes, and complications from multiple studies. IAC requires precise technique, substantial resources, specialized facilities, and retinoblastoma-specific endovascular experience; differences in expertise may contribute to different outcomes between centers. Complication rates are lower than historically, possibly because of improvements in expertise and drug administration. Frequent self-limited ocular effects include periocular edema and hyperemia (34%), ptosis (13.5%), focal madarosis (10.5%), and forehead erythema (3%). In an experienced-team report, Shields et al. found retinal ischemia (1%), choroidal ischemia (1%), and neovascularization of the disc, retina, or iris or glaucoma (approximately 1% each); outcomes differed little by age, race, or sex. Compared with IVC, shorter IAC treatment reduces overall chemotherapy exposure and substantially lowers systemic toxicity. Neutropenia can occur with IAC but is less frequent than with IVC. Potential femoral artery occlusion and blue toe syndrome can be reversed with anticoagulation. Catheterization through the femoral artery, aorta, and carotid artery can cause hematoma or arterial occlusion, and stroke or transient ischemic attack has been reported. Unlike systemic IVC, localized IAC does not provide potential chemotherapy protection elsewhere in the body, so systemic micro-metastatic risk remains in advanced intraocular or extraocular disease. Treatment choice requires weighing these risks and technical demands against the importance of preserving vision for each patient.

document_sections.heading: 4. Intravitreal chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Vitreous seeding is the principal barrier to globe salvage in advanced intraocular retinoblastoma and often accompanies endophytic growth of large undifferentiated tumors. Seeds can contain necrotic cells or viable cells capable of further growth. IVC, IAC, and radiotherapy sometimes help but can fail to eliminate established seeds. Intravitreal chemotherapy (IvitC) began in the 1960 s with thiotepa, although durable outcomes were inconsistent. In 2003, Inomata and Kaneko evaluated 12 anticancer drugs and identified melphalan as the most effective. Suzuki and Kaneko subsequently administered 896 melphalan injections in 237 eyes; only one (0.4%) developed extraocular extension after injection in the presence of dense vitreous seeds and anterior chamber involvement. In 2012, Munier et al. reported effective vitreous-seed control with few adverse effects and no need for external beam irradiation in treated eyes. IvitC is currently mainly a globe-salvage treatment for refractory or recurrent vitreous seeds after other therapies, not a first-line approach. Tumor at the intended injection site, pars plana invasion, and anterior chamber seeding are contraindications. Examination, supported by ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM), is important for safe administration. Melphalan and topotecan are the agents used most often, separately or together; 20–30 μg every 2–4 weeks can control seeds while limiting adverse effects. Injection is generally made through uninvolved pars plana, 2 clock-hours from the seeds and 3–3.5 mm from the limbus, with the needle aimed toward the central vitreous cavity. Munier et al. described an anti-reflux, needle-track sterilization procedure: anterior chamber paracentesis creates transient hypotony before injection with a 32 G needle, followed during needle withdrawal by three freeze-and-thaw cryotherapy cycles at the entry site. Gentle movement of the eye helps distribute the drug and limit local toxicity. The ocular surface is then irrigated with sterile saline and receives topical steroid/antibiotic treatment; a patch and further drops are usually unnecessary. Families are instructed to avoid eye contact for one week. Precision intravitreal chemotherapy (pIvitC), described in 2018 for localized seeds, directs melphalan to the target within 3 mm through the pars plana under indirect ophthalmoscopy. Unlike conventional IvitC, the eye is not moved afterward; head positioning places seeds inferiorly so gravity helps localize drug and limits exposure to the macula and other uninvolved tissue. In 8 treated eyes, seeds completely resolved (100%) after an average of 2.6 injections of 20 μg melphalan, with no recurrence over a mean 10.0 months. The technique is difficult, not widely adopted, and supported by few studied eyes. Shields et al. assessed 40 consecutive eyes with persistent seeds after standard treatment, using intravitreal melphalan (20–30 μg) and topotecan (20 μg) when needed. They reported 100% tumor control with seed regression at a median 3-year followup after 192 injections. In 2023, Abramson and Francis treated recurrent solid retinal tumors in three cases with 90 µg/0.18 cc intravitreal topotecan; a single 90 µg injection resolved each recurrence without associated toxicity. Table 4 summarizes intravitreal agents, doses, globe salvage, and complications reported by individual studies. Local retinal pigment changes at the injection site are the most frequent ocular adverse effect, reported in 18–43% of cases. Higher melphalan doses, especially 50 μg, have been associated with uncommon but serious phthisis bulbi and hypotony, sometimes requiring enucleation. Less common effects include iris or chorioretinal atrophy, transient vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment. Several studies raise concern that melphalan could be more toxic in deeply pigmented eyes, common in Asian populations. This remains speculative and is attributed to potentially greater melphalan uptake and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), retinal, and choroidal injury. Smith et al. analyzed 1304 injections in 315 eyes of 304 patients during 1960 to 2013 and estimated potential IvitC-attributable extraocular dissemination at 0.007%. Francis et al. reported no extraocular tumor extension among 3553 injections in 704 eyes across 10 centers during 1999 to 2017; by the rule of three, estimated risk was no greater than 0.08% per injection. Appropriate patient selection, strict safety procedures, and suitable dosing may keep this risk very low.

document_sections.heading: 5. Intracameral chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Newer treatments have improved globe salvage in advanced retinoblastoma with aqueous seeds. In 2017, Munier et al. introduced intracameral chemotherapy (ICC) as an adjunct to other chemotherapy routes for seed control in unilateral Group E disease, with promising visual outcomes. It offers an alternative to enucleation or anterior chamber plaque radiotherapy, previously the available options when effective chemotherapy delivery to that chamber was difficult. Their original bicameral method treats anterior chamber (AC) and posterior chamber (PC) seeds through a small needle inserted at the peripheral cornea. One-third of the drug enters the AC; the needle then perforates a tumor-free iris-root site to deliver the remaining two-thirds into the PC. Cryotherapy is applied at the entry site. Preoperative ultrasound bio-microscopy can help select that site. Other authors inject only a small amount into the anterior chamber, with or without paracentesis. Clear corneal or limbal delivery of melphalan (15–20 μg/0.05 ml) and topotecan (7.5 μg/0.015 ml) into the anterior and/or posterior chamber has controlled aqueous seeds, with little anterior-segment toxicity and no evidence of extraocular spread in the reported studies. A retrospective study by Munier et al. reported success in 6 out of 11 patients after an average of 4.3 injections. Disruption of the anterior hyaloid face was the main risk factor for failure to retain the eye; reported adverse effects included iris heterochromia and progressive cataract. Borroni et al. also described a one-step aspiration-and-injection approach. ICC is an emerging option for aqueous seeding, but its use requires carefully selected patients and trained, experienced ocular oncologists.

document_sections.heading: 6. Periocular chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Periocular chemotherapy has been used for globe salvage because it reaches high vitreous concentrations within 30 min. It permits doses 6–10 times greater than intravenous delivery and maintains an effect for hours. Periocular carboplatin has been reported, but serious local effects, including orbital fibrosis and optic nerve atrophy, are concerns. Carcaboso et al. first reported periocular topotecan in rabbit models in 2007 and observed high vitreous concentrations, attributed to penetration across the blood-retinal barrier. Later studies supported its efficacy and safety. In 2018, Sthapit et al. reported concurrent periocular topotecan and systemic IVC as safe and effective for vitreous seeds: 63% of 38 eyes achieved complete seed remission. They injected 2 mg (2 ml) of topotecan into the posterior subtenon's space in the inferonasal quadrant using a 27-gauge needle. Delivery methods also include plain liquid, Lincoff balloons, long-acting fibrin sealants, and nanoparticles (NPs). Eyelid edema and conjunctival chemosis after periocular topotecan have been reported but were transient. On current evidence, periocular topotecan is effective and causes fewer complications than carboplatin.

document_sections.heading: 7. Future perspectives
document_sections.content: Phase I trials are assessing sustained-release topotecan delivered by an episcleral plaque, Chemoplaque, for active residual or recurrent retinoblastoma after first-line treatment (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT04156347 and NCT04428879). Safety is their primary outcome and efficacy their secondary outcome. Treatment can still fail despite progress with different chemotherapy routes. Resistance mechanisms are complex and probably differ from resistance to an individual drug. Failure in metastatic disease leaves few treatment options and carries a poor prognosis. Conventional antitumor chemotherapy chiefly disrupts cell division through effects on microtubules needed for the mitotic spindle and on DNA replication. Targeted agents may inhibit proliferation, induce apoptosis, suppress metastasis, alter immune responses, or reverse multidrug resistance. Investigational strategies include molecularly targeted therapies, tubulinmodifying molecules, immunotherapy, high-mobility group A (HMGA) protein, vitamin D analogs, angiogenesis inhibition, neurotransmitter pathway disruption, arsenic trioxide, EDL-155, gene therapy, aqueous humor markers, exosomes, and MLN4924 (pevonedistat). A recent organoid study identified sunitinib as a promising candidate with strong cytotoxicity against classical RB1-deficient and novel MYCN-amplified retinoblastoma organoids; it also inhibited proliferation and induced differentiation. Local delivery systems, particularly nanotechnology, can improve drug bioavailability and targeting. NPs may increase ocular delivery of melphalan while preserving stability, reducing dosing frequency, and permitting sustained, targeted effects. Fibrin glue is also being investigated for injectable chemotherapy delivery, and a dual-layer hydrogel implant shows potential for controlled delivery of low-molecular-weight hydrophilic agents such as topotecan and vincristine. Other investigated intraocular carriers include dendrimers, liposomes, biodegradable polyesters, mesoporous silica, and gold NPs, each with properties potentially useful for individualized treatment. Further research is needed on the long-term consequences of newer targeted and molecular approaches.

document_sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
document_sections.content: Retinoblastoma care requires a multimodal approach that may combine enucleation, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, and thermotherapy. Chemotherapy has been a principal treatment for decades and has improved visual outcomes and survival. It is currently the first-line approach to globe salvage. Choice of delivery route depends on age, stage, laterality, germline status, treatment availability, finances, and family preference. For bilateral or germline disease, IVC is an important primary treatment for intraocular control, metastatic prevention, and reduction of later second malignancies. For unilateral or non-germline disease, IAC is often favored initially because delivery to the affected eye may reduce systemic adverse effects relative to IVC; it is also an option after chemoreduction or other treatment fails. IvitC, ICC, and periocular chemotherapy can supplement treatment in appropriate cases when the required expertise is available. Further chemotherapy development, patient-targeted molecular therapies, and gene therapy may improve vision, particularly in advanced retinoblastoma.
